newsitem.title: ITALY: Parmalat buys Canada's Beatrice Foods.
newsitem.headline: Parmalat buys Canada's Beatrice Foods.

text.p: Italy's largest quoted food group Parmalat Finanziaria took a big step in its international expansion on Friday by snapping up a majority stake in Canada's Beatrice Foods Inc in a deal worth C$290 million.

The Italian milk and dairy products group is allying itself with U.S. bank Citicorp in the deal, with Parmalat paying C$230 for a 75.1 percent in the Canadian food group which has a similar milk and dairy-based product mix to Parmalat.
Citicorp will take the remained 24.9 percent of the group which has a majority of its sales in Canada and the remaining near-20 percent of turnover in the United States.

Parmalat's chairman Calisto Tanzi, who's family own 51 percent of the company, told a news conference that Beatrice Foods was a good opportunity to expand and help internationalise Parmalat's business, which is currently heavily weighed towards Italy and South America.
Parmalat stressed that the cash for the deal will be met out of its own resourcs, and it will not resort to a capital issue or convertible bond issue to finance the acquisition.

A Citicorp spokesman said the bank, as Parmalat's adviser to the deal, was happy to invest in Beatrice Foods and was confident Parmalat's management would improve the Canadian company's performance. Citicorp has already $2 billion of equity stake investments in companies worldwide, he added.
Parmalat said it saw the process of rationalisation already under way in the Canadian dairy sector as positive and it believed this would bring benefits to producers and consumers.

"Parmalat believes the profitability of Beatrice Foods, which is already good, will be able to increase with the introduction of innovative products developed with Parmalat technology," the group said in a statement.
Beatrice Foods had a net operating profit in 1996 of about C$50 million, equal to 5.4 percent of turnover, while it had net financial debt of C$130 million at the end of 1996.

The Canadian group has 23 factories, 20 of which are in its homeland and the other three in the U.S. employing 3,100 people producing fresh milk, yoghurt, cheese, fruit juice and bakery products. Parmalat already has a small business in the U.S. but this acquisition enhances its north American presence.

Parmalat said its own internal 1997 turnover was set to rise 12 percent to 6.1 trillion lire ($3.6 billion) even without Beatrice Foods, but with the Canadian addition it saw turnover at 7.2 trillion lire with a return on sales of over eight percent.

Parmalat reported 1996 results showing annual sales up 27 percent to 5.465 trillion lire, gross operating margins rising 22 percent at 630 billion and net operating margins 27 percent higher at 470 billion. Return on sales was steady at 8.6 percent.
It added that 38 percent of its turnover was in Italy and the remaining 62 percent abroad, while it added that its net debt at end-1996 totalled 802 billion lire.
Parmalat said the deal was expected to be closed towards mid-April once approval was obtained from the relevant authorities. ($1=1,688 lire)
